name: Black feminism
summary: Black feminism holds that racism, sexism, class exploitation and heterosexism interlock in Black women's lives, so neither the white women's movement nor Black liberation movements that ignore gender can free them. Its main texts are socialist and anti-capitalist, defend abortion rights and oppose forced sterilization, reject separatism from Black men, and treat Black women's own experience as a source of knowledge and politics.
scope: The US Black feminist tradition from the late 1960s: Beal's 'Double Jeopardy' and the Third World Women's Alliance, the Combahee River Collective Statement (1977), Lorde, Crenshaw's intersectionality articles, Collins's Black Feminist Thought, Davis's Women, Race & Class and Are Prisons Obsolete?, and hooks. Positions that these texts do not state, including most of the wider left's agenda, are left null; liberal strands (the NBFO, which Combahee called bourgeois-feminist) and womanist theology are not covered by the sources opened.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The Combahee statement commits the Collective to an integrated analysis because racial, sexual, heterosexual and class oppression are interlocking, and Collins's matrix of domination and Crenshaw's intersectionality say the same.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Combahee holds that sexual politics under patriarchy is as pervasive in Black women's lives as race and class, and hooks defines the aim as ending patriarchal domination.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Combahee says liberation requires destroying capitalism and imperialism as well as patriarchy, and Beal says women's oppression serves as an escape valve for capitalism.

abortion-legal.rationale: Beal says the right to decide whether and when to have children must not be given up and calls rigid abortion laws a means of subjugation; Combahee members worked on abortion rights and hooks treats reproductive rights as central.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Combahee rejects the Black nationalist claim that men lead the house and women are different by nature, and Beal calls telling women to take a domestic, submissive role counter-revolutionary.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Combahee presents the male-headed home as the assumption feminism calls into question, saying sex should not decide who holds power, and Beal asks revolutionaries to treat wives and husbands as equals.

traditional-family.rationale: Collins calls the nuclear family with a breadwinner husband far from natural, universal or preferred, and Beal rejects the housewife model; hooks nevertheless calls feminism pro-family, so the answer is mild.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Combahee says racism is a pervasive factor in Black women's lives and names racial oppression one of the systems it fights; Collins and hooks write of an ongoing new racism and white supremacist capitalist patriarchy.

race-social-construct.rationale: Crenshaw says that race and gender are socially constructed categories, while insisting that this does not make them insignificant.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Crenshaw treats gender as a socially constructed category, and Combahee calls any biological determinism a dangerous and reactionary basis for politics.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Crenshaw treats race as a social construction and Combahee rejects biological determinism as reactionary, which leaves no room for a genetic account of group differences.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Crenshaw's 1989 critique of treating white women's experience as women's experience and her 1991 point that identity politics conflates intragroup differences argue against one fixed category of women.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Collins argues that knowledge is part of the social relations of domination, that dominant groups impose their own specialized thought, and that Black women's standpoint produces a different, subjugated knowledge.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Collins says domination works by seducing and pressuring subordinate people to adopt the dominant group's thought through schools, churches and media, not only by force.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Collins names the media among the institutions that spread the dominant group's thought and require docility, and her Sexual Politics chapter treats images of Black women as serving domination.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Combahee begins from the belief that Black women are inherently valuable and asks only to be recognised as human, levelly human, and Crenshaw argues for equal protection of Black women under the law.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Combahee, Beal and Davis all treat the legacy of slavery and Jim Crow as something to be fought against actively, with anti-racist struggle a core commitment.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Davis's history treats Jim Crow segregation and lynch law as a system of racist enslavement that Black women resisted, and Combahee commits to fighting racial oppression.

racial-franchise.rationale: Davis recounts Black women's fight for the vote and the disfranchisement of Black voters as part of Jim Crow, treating them as injustices.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Collins describes laws against intermarriage as tools that contained and exploited Black sexuality as deviant.

women-suffrage.rationale: Davis's history treats the vote as a right that Black and working women fought for and condemns the racism that shaped the suffrage movement.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Collins presents laws forbidding gay and lesbian marriage as part of the system of sexual control, and Combahee fights heterosexual oppression.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Combahee commits to struggling against heterosexual oppression as a lesbian and Black feminist collective, and Collins describes homophobia as oppression that kills.

revolution-justified.rationale: Combahee sees revolutionary change as its task and a socialist, feminist and anti-racist revolution as its aim, and Beal speaks of armed struggle and a people's revolution.

political-violence-never.rationale: Beal writes of men preparing for armed struggle and of the willingness to die in revolution as part of the liberation struggle, and does not reject political violence.

means-match-ends.rationale: Combahee says it does not believe the end justifies the means and commits to collective process and nonhierarchical power in the group and in its vision of a revolutionary society.

gradual-change.rationale: Combahee calls itself revolutionary and wants all systems of oppression destroyed, and Beal says black women cannot wait for the revolution to deal with their own problems.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Combahee values collective process and nonhierarchical power in its organising and its vision of a revolutionary society, and Collins stresses community-based power from below.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Combahee wants work organised for the benefit of those who do it rather than for the profit of bosses and is in essential agreement with Marx on the economic relationships he analysed; Beal describes Black women as economically exploited.

production-for-use.rationale: Combahee says work must be organised for the collective benefit of those who do the work and create the products, and not for the profit of the bosses.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Combahee calls itself socialist and aims to destroy capitalism, and Collins contrasts a market model of community built on competition with Black women's model of caring connection.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Beal says capitalism set out to destroy the humanity of Black people, and Combahee names capitalism as a system of oppression to be destroyed.

property-fundamental.rationale: Combahee holds that material resources must be equally distributed among those who create them and that work must be organised for collective benefit, which a near-inviolable property right would contradict.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Combahee states that material resources must be equally distributed among those who create them.

unions-good.rationale: Davis praises Black women unionists and Combahee names workplace organising as work it would do, while Beal condemns the white male leadership of unions for racism and chauvinism.

cut-welfare.rationale: hooks calls the dismantling of the welfare system a betrayal of feminist issues that creates a new underclass of women and children, and Combahee lists welfare among its organising concerns.

work-for-welfare.rationale: hooks says workfare-oriented welfare, with the prison industry and immigration policy, creates conditions for indentured slavery for poor women.

socialized-care.rationale: Stated by Angela Davis alone in the sources read; no other Black feminist source shows the tradition shares it.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Davis condemns the eugenic call for compulsory sterilization of the unfit, and Beal calls pressure on poor Black women to be sterilized surgical genocide.

limit-population.rationale: Beal treats campaigns to curb the numbers of poor and non-white people as genocide while defending voluntary family planning, and Davis likewise condemns population control as racist.

death-penalty.rationale: Stated by Angela Davis alone in the sources read; no other Black feminist source shows the tradition shares it.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Stated by Angela Davis alone in the sources read; no other Black feminist source shows the tradition shares it.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Stated by Angela Davis alone in the sources read; no other Black feminist source shows the tradition shares it.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Combahee holds that Black women should organise around their own identity and shares solidarity with Black men around race, though it rejects the same politics for white women's separatism.

racial-pride.rationale: Combahee grounds its politics in a healthy love for Black women and their community, and Collins calls for valuing Black women's own self-definition.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Third World Women's Alliance platform demands that healthcare and other services necessary to survival be free for the masses, and the Combahee Collective names defending a Third World community's hospital care among its causes; neither text says it should be provided by the government as such.

missingStatements.text: The most radical politics come from the experience of one's own oppressed group rather than from working to end someone else's oppression.
missingStatements.rationale: Combahee states identity politics as its core principle.

missingStatements.text: Poor and non-white women should not be pressured or forced into sterilization or birth control.
missingStatements.rationale: Beal, Davis and Combahee all campaign against sterilization abuse while defending voluntary birth control.

missingStatements.text: Women of colour who face both race and sex discrimination should be able to bring their claim as a distinct group, not as race or sex claims separately.
missingStatements.rationale: Crenshaw's 1989 critique of antidiscrimination doctrine, shared by Collins.

missingStatements.text: Women should struggle alongside men of their own racial group against racism while also struggling against those men's sexism, rather than separating from them.
missingStatements.rationale: Combahee rejects separatism and states this double struggle; Beal says the same of Black men.

missingStatements.text: Healthcare, housing, food, clothing, transportation and education should be free and controlled by the people who use them.
missingStatements.rationale: The Third World Women's Alliance platform demands exactly this for the masses of Third World people.

notes: Searched all ten themes in these texts; economy, society and liberty hold most answers, government, world, ecology and technology are almost wholly silent in the sources. Answers resting on Davis alone (death penalty, legalizing drugs and sex work, socialized care) rest on one defining thinker; the Combahee/NBFO split (socialist vs liberal) and Beal's 1969 Black Power context are the main strand differences. Not opened: the NBFO statement of purpose, Black Women's Manifesto, Collins's full Black Feminist Thought, Lorde's Sister Outsider, hooks's Ain't I a Woman. Deepen pass 2026-10-30: Lorde's Sister Outsider read in full and the Third World Women's Alliance's platform (archive.org pamphlet) added. Themes searched: economy, health, employment, income, education, family and reproduction, sexuality, anti-imperialism, war, police, prison, welfare. Lorde-only positions (the erotic and work, Grenada and non-intervention, female circumcision, anger) stay null because no other Black feminist source states them; Davis-only positions (prisons, death penalty, drugs, sex work) stay null. Blocked: Combahee's other texts and the Home Girls and All the Women Are White anthologies (lending-only on archive.org), the Black Woman's Manifesto as a page (the Dartmouth copy is images; its platform is in the Alliance pamphlet).
